intro.carita: Madhyama Carita (the middle episode), of which this is the battle chapter. In the recitation tradition the middle carita’s presiding form is Mahālakṣmī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 2), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 3 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna: the Goddess with the radiance of a thousand rising suns, in red silk, wearing a garland of heads, her breasts reddened, holding in her lotus hands a rosary, vidyā (usually understood as a book), the gesture of fearlessness and the boon, three-eyed, her crown bound with the moon, seated on a lotus.
intro.summary: Medhas goes on with the story (3.1). Seeing the army cut down, Mahiṣa’s general Cikṣura goes out to fight Ambikā and rains arrows on her like a cloud on Meru (3.2–3). She cuts his arrows to pieces as if at play, kills his horses and charioteer, breaks his bow and standard and pierces him (3.4–5); on foot with sword and shield he strikes the lion on the head and the Goddess on her arm, and the sword shatters (3.6–8). His flaming spear, hurled at Bhadrakālī, is broken by hers, and he dies with it (3.9–10). Cāmara comes on an elephant: his lance falls to her ‘hum’, his spear to her arrows (3.11–13), and the lion leaps onto the elephant, crashes to the ground with him and strikes off his head (3.14–16). The remaining generals fall in a catalogue — Udagra, Karāla, Uddhata, Bāṣkala, Tāmra, Andhaka, Ugrāsya, Ugravīrya, Mahāhanu, Biḍāla, Durdhara, Durmukha — each with the weapon that kills him (3.17–20). Mahiṣa himself, in his own buffalo shape, tramples the Goddess’s hosts with muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, speed, bellowing and breath (3.21–23), charges her lion (3.24), and in his rage breaks the earth, floods the ocean, tears the clouds and sends mountains crashing from the sky (3.25–27). Caṇḍikā turns her wrath to his death (3.28): she binds him with her noose; he sheds the buffalo and becomes a lion, then a man with a sword, then an elephant, each cut down in turn, and then the buffalo again, shaking the three worlds (3.29–33). She drinks and laughs, he flings mountains, and grinding them to dust she speaks (3.34–36): ‘Roar, fool, for a moment, while I drink; when I have slain you the gods will roar’ (3.37–38). She leaps on him, presses his neck with her foot and strikes him with her spear (3.39–40); caught half out of the buffalo’s mouth, still fighting, he is beheaded with her great sword (3.41–42). The asura army perishes, the gods rejoice and praise her, the Gandharvas sing and the Apsarases dance (3.43–44).
intro.forms: Ambikā, ‘the Mother’, the narrator’s commonest name for her (3.2, 3.12, 3.24, 3.30); Bhadrakālī, ‘the auspicious Kālī’ (3.9); Trinetrā, the three-eyed, and Parameśvarī, the Supreme Sovereign (3.19); Mahādevī (3.24); Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce one’, from the turning point onward (3.28, 3.34, 3.35); and Jaganmātā, Mother of the world, in the moment of her fiercest act (3.34). Her final act — foot on the buffalo’s neck, spear and sword (3.40–42) — is the image painted and sculpted as Mahiṣāsuramardinī, a name the chapter itself does not use. Her lion and her hosts (gaṇas) fight as hers throughout (3.14–16, 3.21–24).
intro.significance: This is the battle the middle carita was building to: the Goddess made from the gods’ combined radiance in chapter 2 now does alone what the gods could not. The chapter moves outward in scale — a chariot duel, a wrestling match, a catalogue of deaths, then a buffalo whose rage reaches earth, ocean and sky (3.25–27) — and then inward to a single image: the asura caught halfway out of his own body (3.41). The gods take no part in the fighting; their part is joy and praise (3.43–44), which becomes the hymn of chapter 4 (4.2).
intro.grammar: A long run of reduplicated perfects as the narrative tense (ववर्ष, जघान, चिच्छेद, विव्याध, पफाल, जग्राह, चिक्षेप); periphrastic perfects of causatives (पातयामास, त्रासयामास, प्लावयामास, क्षोभयामास); passive narration with the agent in the instrumental (मृगारिणा … पृथक्कृतम्, 3.16; तया … देव्या … निपातितः, 3.42); locative absolutes (3.11, 3.21, 3.38); यावत् … तावत् with the present for an act about to happen (3.30); duals for the lion and Cāmara (3.15); a verse without a verb that waits for the next (3.22–23); and, in the Goddess’s one speech, the imperative and the future of the same root (गर्ज … गर्जिष्यन्ति, 3.38). Two verbs show the Purāṇic ātmanepada for the active (अमुञ्चत, 3.10; निरकृन्तत, 3.32).
intro.teaching: Literally, the chapter is a battle: generals die one by one, a buffalo-asura changes shape and is killed, and the gods celebrate. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the Goddess’s ease as the point — she cuts his arrows ‘as if at play’ (3.4), a sword breaks on her arm (3.8), a lance falls to a sound (3.12), and she drinks and laughs before the kill (3.34), so that the outcome is never in doubt (3.38). Modern readers often add a reflection of their own: an adversary that escapes by changing its shape (3.29–33) is overcome only when it is caught in the middle of the change (3.41–42), and the pride that roars (3.35, 3.38) is given its moment and no more. These readings are interpretations; the text itself states only the battle and the gods’ joy.
themes: The ease (līlā) of the Goddess in battle
The lion and the gaṇas: those who fight as hers
Mahiṣa’s rage at the scale of the world
Shape-changing and the escape that fails
Two intoxications: her drink and his pride
Victory turned into the gods’ praise

conclusion.narrative: Mahiṣa’s generals come out one at a time and die one at a time — Cikṣura in a chariot duel, Cāmara under the lion’s paw, the rest in a single catalogue. Then Mahiṣa himself fights as a buffalo, and his rage reaches earth, sea and sky. Caṇḍikā binds him; he slips from form to form — lion, man, elephant, buffalo again — until, with her foot on his neck, he is caught halfway out of the buffalo and beheaded. The chapter ends with what she promised in her one speech: the gods rejoicing, and the sound of praise (3.43–44), which chapter 4 takes up as a hymn.

vocabulary.en: ‘the auspicious Kālī’, a name of the Goddess
the sound ‘hum’, used as a weapon
hosts, the Goddess’s troops born from her breath
the drink (wine, mead) the Goddess drinks

constructions: The reduplicated perfect as the tense of narrative, singular and plural (जघान, चिच्छेद, विव्याध; ययुः, निपेतुः, तुष्टुवुः, ननृतुः).
The periphrastic perfect in -आमास for causatives and class-10 stems (पातयामास, त्रासयामास, चूर्णयामास, क्षोभयामास).
Passive narration: the past participle as verb, the agent in the instrumental (करप्रहारेण शिरश्चामरस्य पृथक्कृतम्, 3.16; देव्या … हतः, 3.17; तया … निपातितः, 3.42).
The locative absolute for the time of an action (हते तस्मिन् … चमूपतौ, 3.11; स्वसैन्ये संक्षीयमाणे, 3.21; मया त्वयि हते, 3.38).
यावत् … तावत् with the present for an act on the point of happening (3.30), and यावत् alone with the present for an act that runs alongside (3.38).
Distributive pronouns (कांश्चित् … अपरान् … अन्यान्) with instrumentals of means, gathered by one verb across two verses (3.22–23).
A chain of absolutives and a participle leading to one finite verb (उक्त्वा, समुत्पत्य, आरूढा, आक्रम्य … अताडयत्, 3.40).
The imperative and the future of one root set against each other (गर्ज गर्ज … गर्जिष्यन्ति, 3.38).
insights: Nothing the asuras bring reaches her: arrows are cut ‘as if at play’ (3.4), a sword shatters on her arm (3.8), a lance falls to a single sound (3.12).

The Goddess fights through what is hers: the lion kills Cāmara (3.14–16), the gaṇas born from her breath bear Mahiṣa’s first assault (3.21–23), and it is the attack on her lion that turns her anger on him (3.24, 3.32).

The asura’s disorder is cosmic, not private: earth, ocean, clouds and mountains suffer (3.25–27), and the three worlds tremble again when he resumes the buffalo (3.33) — which is why the one who acts is named Mother of the world (3.34).
Escape by changing form is answered form by form (3.29–33) and ends when he is caught between forms (3.41–42).
Her intoxication and his stand face to face: she drinks and laughs (3.34, 3.38), he is ‘drunk with pride’ (बलवीर्यमदोद्धतः, 3.35) and cannot see what he fights.
The victory belongs to the gods only as joy and praise (3.38, 3.43–44); the praise becomes the next chapter’s hymn (4.2).
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares a few names and images with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Parameśvarī (3.19; name 396, परमेश्वरी), Caṇḍikā (3.28, 3.34, 3.35; name 755, चण्डिका), the red eyes of the drinking Goddess (3.34; compare name 432, मदघूर्णितरक्ताक्षी), her taste for madhu (3.38; compare name 510, मधुप्रीता), and the noose (3.29), which the Lalitā Sahasranāma gives its own meaning, attachment (name 8, रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या). These are a shared Śākta vocabulary, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The battle with Mahiṣa belongs to the Devī Māhātmya alone, and no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: She cuts Cikṣura’s arrows to pieces ‘as if at play’ (लीलयैव) and kills his horses and charioteer.
Ambikā brings Cāmara’s lance to the ground, its fire gone, with the sound ‘hum’ alone.
She binds the great asura with her noose; caught, he sheds his buffalo form — the transformations begin.
Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the world, in fury drinks the supreme drink again and again and laughs, her eyes red.
‘Roar, fool, roar for a moment while I drink’ — the Goddess’s only speech: the gods will roar when he is slain.
Pinned by her foot, the asura is caught half-emerged from the buffalo’s mouth, held by her power.
Still half emerged and still fighting, he is struck down by the Goddess, who cuts off his head with her great sword.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is the commonest junction: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (ततो देवी), -ḥ → s/ś before t/c (ततस्तौ, सेनानीश्चिक्षुरः), -ḥ → r before vowels and voiced sounds (बाणैर्यन्तारं), and the special rule for सः (स देवीं, 3.3; सच्छिन्नधन्वा, 3.6).
-aḥ before a vowel other than a loses its visarga and leaves the vowels apart (तत एवाशु, 3.31; अर्धनिष्क्रान्त एवासीद्, 3.41; अर्धनिष्क्रान्त एवासौ, 3.42).

Pūrvarūpa with avagraha (समरेऽसुरः, सोऽभून्महागजः), once on a dual verb that strict grammar would leave pragṛhya (युयुधातेऽतिसंरब्धौ, 3.15, kept as ārṣa); ā + ā written with the double avagraha (साऽऽरूढा, 3.40; पदाऽऽक्रान्तः, 3.41).

Consonant sandhi: t + ś → cch (तच्छूलं, 3.10), ch doubled after a short vowel (तस्यच्छित्त्वा, 3.4), t → n before nasals (तस्मान्नागान्महीं, 3.15), and n before c and ś (-आंश्च, -आञ्छृ-, 3.22, where the Gita Press spells out what the witnesses leave unapplied).
Optional visarga kept before a sibilant (मेरुगिरेः शृङ्गं, 3.3; ततः सिंहः, 3.14); savarṇa-dīrgha, guṇa and vṛddhi across words and inside compounds (लीलयैव, शरोत्करान्).
samasa: Bahuvrīhis of loss in a row (छिन्नधन्वा, विरथः, हताश्वः, हतसारथिः, 3.5–6), with धनुस् replaced by धन्वन् at the end of a bahuvrīhi.
Bahuvrīhis as epithets and names (त्रिनेत्रा, अरुणलोचना, खड्गपाणिः; the generals उग्रास्य, उग्रवीर्य, महाहनु, दुर्मुख).
Upapada tatpuruṣas with verbal roots (सेनानीः, तोयदः, तुरगान्, आशुगैः, त्रिदशार्दनः, भूधरान्).
Nested tṛtīyā tatpuruṣas of cause in the cosmic verses (वेगभ्रमणविक्षुण्णा, धुतशृङ्गविभिन्नाः, श्वासानिलास्ताः, 3.26–27).
Dvandvas: samāhāra खड्गचर्मणा (3.31, neuter singular), itaretara दन्तमुष्टितलैः (3.17), and a dvandva inside सचराचरम् (3.33).
Karmadhārayas with महा- (महासुरः, महामृधे, महागजः, महासिना), and the long adverbial bahuvrīhi मदोद्धूतमुखरागाकुलाक्षरम् (3.36).
grammar_notes: Purāṇic ātmanepada for the active: अमुञ्चत (3.10) and निरकृन्तत (3.32), the latter from a parasmaipada root; neither is a passive.
The genitive marks the target of a throw where the locative would be stricter: देव्याः with मुमोच (3.12), तस्य with पाशं क्षिप्त्वा (3.29).
Verbs carried across lines and verses: the second line of 3.18 is governed by जघान in 3.19; 3.22 waits for पातयामास in 3.23; स च महासुरः (3.10) supplies नीतः from नीतम्.
The same participle is printed युद्ध्यमानौ (3.15) and युध्यमानः (3.42); the doubled stop is the Gita Press’s spelling, not another form.
Active past participles of motion and posture taking objects: तं महासुरम् आरूढा (3.40), माहिषं वपुः आस्थितः (3.33).
themes: Līlā: the ease of the Goddess
The lion and the gaṇas as hers
uncertain: 3.15: युद्ध्यमानौ (Gita Press) / युध्यमानौ (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic; the same form.
3.22: चान्याञ्छृङ्गाभ्यां (Gita Press) / चान्यान्शृङ्गाभ्यां (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic; the sandhi spelled out or left unapplied.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading, are flagged on 3.12 (देव्याः as target of मुमोच or with हुंकाराभिहताम्), 3.36 (whether the flushed face is the Goddess’s or the asura’s) and 3.41 (देव्याः or देव्या with वीर्येण).
The Purāṇa recension in GRETIL’s Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa carries further verses in 3.21 and 3.43 that the Gita Press Saptaśatī does not; nothing was added (corrections.json, recension notes).
